title: You Should Care Less About Practical Advice
author: Scott H. Young
summary: Scott Young argues that anyone who cares about usefulness should spend most of their learning time on fundamental principles rather than practical tips. He uses a tree of knowledge as a model: principles form the trunk, branching points split by circumstance, and practical advice is the leaves, which are numerous and each cover only a narrow set of situations. He applies the idea to getting fit, starting a business and studying, noting that a workout plan built for a young athlete can be counterproductive for a 55-year-old recovering from injury. He answers three objections: that principles underdetermine decisions, that some principles are undiscovered, and that deriving practice from principles can be intractable. His practical conclusion is to read the trunks of many domains, through textbooks or general-reader introductions, before reaching for advice books.
points: Knowledge works like a tree in which principles are the trunk and practical tips are the many narrow leaves.
Specific advice helps only if your situation matches the one it was designed for, while principles transfer across situations.
Principles often do not fully determine a decision, but they still tell you where to look, like knowing which branch a bird is on.
In domains where principles are undiscovered or hard to apply, practical advice must fill the gap, though principles remain worth learning.
Readers should favor textbooks and general introductions over advice books once they plan to read more than one book on a topic.
quotes: If you care about usefulness, spending most of your time learning “advice” or “tips” is counterproductive.
